sections.heading: Mizoram- Handicrafts - Cane and Bamboo Work
sections.content: The Mizos expertise in wicker-work and basketry is well known. Even their houses are generally built with bamboo walls and floors and thatched roofs. While women excel at weaving, men are expert at cane and bamboo work. They make fine cane hats and uncommonly beautiful baskets. The traditional Mizo hat is known for its workmanship. The fine woven bamboo hat looks as fine as cotton yarn. A typical Mizo basket is broad at the rim and tapers at the bottom. There are baskets for carrying firewood, water, paddy, rice and vegetables. Baskets made of cane and bamboo together with leaves and grasses, for storing ornaments, clothes and other valuables are also made. Bamboo is also used in traditional ornaments. while celebrations, Mizo women use a headgear of a bamboo band with parrot feathers stuck in it, the ends of which are decorated with beetles. Other bamboo products include fish and animal traps, rain bamboo hat seen with the formation of a flat thin layer on its top, japis, cones, circular boxes and other materials serving as reservoirs and containers of goods, crops and other things. Both Mizo men and women love their locally made pipes. The womens pipe is like a small hukkah, small enough to be easily held in the hand and carried about. The mens pipe is of western type. These are made out of bamboo and weed.

sections.heading: Mizoram- Handicrafts- Basketry
sections.content: Basketry among the Mizo is a delicate work. They are experts in making etches and notches from the soft fibres of cane. Baskets with lids and without lids, smoothly surfaced, strongly floored, gently fenced from mouth to base and modelled into oval, square, flat structures, revealing a considerable skill in slitting, folding and inserting are seen. They serve various purposes such as cages, containers, baskets of different articles, etc. Some forms of baskets made in Mizoram are dawrawn, empai, emping, tlamen, paikawng, hnam, paiem, fawng, thul, etc.

sections.heading: Weaving
sections.content: is an integral part of the Mizo culture and the women learn how to weave at an early age. Puans in numerous designs are produced by them on traditional looms. These are somewhat like lungis worn by the women, and are their native dress. Puans are noted for their beautiful design and intricate embroidery which is invariably worked out along with the weave. Mizos have a wealth of motifs. Mizo women also make attractive shawls and shoulder bags. The Hmars weave many designs and some of the important ones are thangsuo puon meaning famous cloth, puon laisen meaning cloth with red in the middle, hmarm - the loin cloth worn by women and zakuolaisen - the blouse piece used mainly by the unmarried girls.

sections.heading: Mizoram- Fairs and Festivals
sections.content: The festivals of Mizoram are related to the agricultural activities that bring forth the vibrancy and the liveliness of the people of Mizoram. Some of the major festivals in Mizoram which can be mentioned are Chapchar Kut, Mim Kut, Pawl Kut and Thalfavang Kut.

sections.heading: Mizoram- Fairs and Festivals- Chapchar Kut
sections.content: Chapchar Kut, the spring festival is the most important in Mizoram. People of all ages, men and women, dress themselves in traditional and colourful costumes and wear exotic headgears and jewellery. They assemble and perform various folk dances and also sing traditional songs accompanied by beating of drums, gongs and cymbals. The groups from every region come to the event and display their best performance. The performers dance in joyous celebration of life. Cheraw or the bamboo dance which is popular all over the country is also performed during this festival. The Mizo dances are associated with their respective festival celebrations. More popular dances like the Cheraw are performed almost in every festival of the state.

sections.heading: Mizoram- Fairs and Festivals- Thalfavang Kut
sections.content: When the farmers complete the process of weeding of the field and prepare for the forthcoming harvest, the Thalfavang Kut festival takes place. This colourful festival gives the community an opportunity to come together, retain the present bonds and renew the old ones.

sections.heading: Mizoram- Fairs and Festivals- Christmas
sections.content: Christmas is celebrated for three days from twenty fourth to tweny sixth December every year. The majority of the population in Mizoram follows Christianity. On Christmas Eve, the people start celebration in their homes and on Christmas, a grand celebration takes place in the church. Next day the people have a grand and sumptuous feast where everyone from young to old take part and rejoice with great fervour and festivities.

sections.heading: Mizoram- Performing Art- Khuallam Dance
sections.content: Khuallam (Dance of the Guests) is a dance performed during the ceremony called Khuangchawi. During this ceremony, the invited guest enters the area dancing Khuallam. Hand-woven Mizo cloth known as Puandum is wrapped over the shoulders and the dance is performed by swaying the cloth. It has the colours of black, red, yellow and green stripes and is a significant cloth in their culture as every girl takes along this cloth when she gets married. When the husband dies this cloth is used for covering his body.

sections.heading: Cheraw Dance
sections.content: One of the most popular folk dance traditions of Mizoram is Cheraw. Men sitting on the ground face to face, dance by tapping long bamboo staves and they open and close it up in rhythmic beats. sections.heading: State Museum
sections.content: The Mizoram State Museum exhibits a wide array of costumes, artifacts and historical relics. Glimpses on the traditional clothes, artifacts and historical relics can reveal much of the culture and the heritage of the Mizo people. Some of the weapons that are displayed here have been used in battles fought many years ago. From time immemorial, the Mizo craftsmanship had been recognised by their work in bamboo and cane craft. The best skills of Mizoram craft can be depicted in weaving, pipes, jewellery, musical instruments, bamboo and cane craft. Weaving is an integral part of Mizo life.
